Simulations

Type I error

At \(\alpha = 5\%\), Bradley’s liberal robustness criterion treats empirical rejection rates between \(2.5\%\) and \(7.5\%\) as acceptable [@Bradley:1978]. Abbreviations are: F = Fisher’s one-way ANOVA; W = Welch’s heteroscedastic ANOVA; L = Levene gate selecting F or W; KW = Kruskal–Wallis; SW = Shapiro–Wilk gate selecting W or KW; SW+L = Shapiro–Wilk gate selecting KW or, if the parametric branch is retained, Levene gate selecting F or W. In the Type I simulations, \(n\) denotes the common per-group sample size in balanced rows; in unbalanced rows, \(\bar n\) denotes the mean per-group sample size. The unbalanced group sizes are \[ (n_1,n_2,n_3,n_4)\approx\bar n(0.5,0.8,1.2,1.5), \] rounded to the nearest integers; therefore the realised mean group size is not guaranteed to equal exactly \(\bar n\).

In contrast to the normal distribution, where mean and variance are independent parameters, this is not the case for the Gamma distribution \(G \sim \Gamma(\alpha,\theta)\), with shape parameter \(\alpha>0\) and scale parameter \(\theta>0\). The mean is \(E(G)=\alpha\theta\), whereas the variance is \(\mathrm{Var}(G)=\alpha\theta^2\). The corresponding skewness is \(2/\sqrt{\alpha}\), and the kurtosis is \(3+6/\alpha\), so the excess kurtosis is \(6/\alpha\) [@Forbes:2010, p. 109]. In the simulations, \(\theta=1\) and \(\alpha\in\{16,4,1,0.25\}\), followed by standardisation \(Z=(G-\alpha\theta)/(\theta\sqrt{\alpha})\).

In the identical-distribution setting, both relevant null hypotheses are true: equal means for F, W, and L, and equal rank distributions for KW; SW and SW+L both remain within Bradley bounds in all conditions, showing that the automatic route does not inflate rejection when both candidate null hypotheses are true (Figure @ref(fig:route1-identical-typeI)).

In the unequal-distribution setting, the equal-means null remains true, but the Kruskal–Wallis null is false because group distributions differ in spread; hence standalone Kruskal–Wallis is not part of the mean-null Type I comparison. Welch has fewer Bradley-bound violations than Fisher and the Levene-gated route, so the Levene variance gate adds little as a Fisher/Welch decision rule. The full SW gate often routes to Kruskal–Wallis under skewness, which is defensible only if the automatic procedure is read as a visible switch from testing means to testing rank distributions (Figure @ref(fig:route1-unequal-mean-null-rejection)).

Power simulations

Power was estimated as the rejection probability under ordered location shifts of 0, 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75 SD across four balanced homoscedastic groups. In the normal and mildly skewed cases, the parametric routes have the highest power; in strongly skewed cases, Kruskal–Wallis becomes dominant. The SW+L route follows this switch and is equal or closest to the best-performing strategy across skewness levels. In the normal four-group corner, the small Fisher advantage over Welch follows directly from Eq. @ref(eq:welch-anova-four-groups), \(\frac{F}{F_W}=1+3/[5(n-1)]\) (Figure @ref(fig:route1-power-skew-sweep)). Here \(n\) denotes the per-group sample size; the total sample size is \(N=4n\).

Power simulation under ordered additive group shifts of 0, 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75 SD. The y-axis shows the simulated rejection rate at alpha = 5% for six strategies across skewness and per-group sample size n; total sample size is N = 4n. The data-generating difference is only additive: group means are shifted by 0, 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75 SD. Abbreviations: F = Fisher; W = Welch; L = Levene gate; KW = Kruskal–Wallis; SW = Shapiro–Wilk gate selecting W or KW; SW+L = Shapiro–Wilk gate selecting KW or, if the parametric branch is retained, Levene gate selecting F or W. Bottom labels show SW+L gate decisions. Kruskal–Wallis tests ranks; pairwise stochastic equality corresponds to P(X_i > X_j) + 0.5 P(X_i = X_j) = 0.5. Skew = 0 is normal; skew > 0 uses standardised Gamma groups, where skewness and excess kurtosis vary together. The high-skew result is not a contradiction of the CLT: for fixed mean differences, increasing N makes the mean-based tests valid and eventually highly powered even under strong skewness; KW may also approach 100% power because the location shift changes the ordering of observations.

Taken together, the simulations support keeping SW+L as the automatic route. This keeps the paper’s general linear model framing coherent: if standardised residual normality is not rejected, homoscedasticity decides whether the analysis remains with Fisher’s ANOVA or moves to Welch’s ANOVA. In the power simulation, the Levene layer shows no power loss relative to SW; under true homoscedasticity it recovers Fisher’s small-sample advantage over Welch at \(n=10\) and \(n=20\), as expected from Eq. @ref(eq:welch-anova-four-groups). The cost is not power but interpretation: under unequal distributions with equal means, SW+L increasingly reports the rejection rate of KW after the hypothesis switch, so that row must not be read as a Type I error rate for equal means.

If all groups really come from the same distribution, all methods stay close to the intended 5% false-alarm rate, and the automatic SW and SW+L routes behave well. If the groups have the same mean but different spreads, Welch is the cleanest test for the equal-means question; Fisher and the Levene gate are less stable. The SW routes switch to Kruskal–Wallis very early, even at mild skew or unequal spread, so they are useful as an automatic method switch, but not as a pure test of equal means.

If all groups really come from the same distribution, all methods stay close to the intended 5% false-alarm rate, and the automatic SW and SW+L routes behave well. If the groups have the same mean but different spreads, Welch is the cleanest test for the equal-means question; Fisher and the Levene gate are less stable. The SW routes switch to Kruskal–Wallis very early, even at mild skew or unequal spread, so they are useful as an automatic method switch, but not as a pure test of equal means.

Read as an equal-means simulation, the results mainly support Welch. From about \(\bar n = 50\), Welch stays within Bradley’s bounds even at skew = 6 when the larger groups also have the larger standard deviations. When larger standard deviations occur in the smaller groups, the difficult case moves upward: Welch needs about \(\bar n = 100\) at skew = 6, with no simulated value between 50 and 100. Thus, even in very skewed settings, the central limit effect can be sufficient for the equal-means question, which argues for Welch as the stable default if the estimand is the mean.

#Simulation errors The Monte Carlo standard error of an estimated rejection rate \(\hat p\) from \(B\) simulation runs is

\[ SE_{\mathrm{MC}}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{B}} . \]

Here, each simulation cell used \(B = 50000\) repetitions. For a rejection rate near the nominal level, \(\hat p = 5\%\),

\[ SE_{\mathrm{MC}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.05(1-0.05)}{50000}} = 0.10\%. \]

The Monte Carlo standard error is maximal at \(\hat p = 50\%\), where it equals \(0.22\%\).
